opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the goal is pretty simple to state and very hard to achieve: we want every software engineer to feel like they have a team of really capable collaborators working alongside them. Not a tool you have to babysit, but something you can hand a real task to, like "go fix this bug," "write the tests for this module," or "migrate this service," and it actually goes off, does the work, and comes back with something you can review and merge.

If you look at what engineers spend their time on, a huge fraction isn't the creative, high-leverage part. It's the toil: chasing down flaky tests, reading through unfamiliar code to understand why something breaks, upgrading dependencies, writing boilerplate. Those are the things that drain people. What I'd love is for Codex to absorb more and more of that, so humans can focus on the parts that need judgment and taste: what should we build, how should the system be architected, what does the user actually need.

And I think it changes who gets to build software, too. Right now there's a big gap between having an idea and being able to realize it in code. If we can shrink that gap, many more people can create things, and the people who are already great engineers become dramatically more productive. It's about amplifying what people can do, not replacing the human in the loop.

So the north star for me is that software engineering becomes much more about intent and much less about mechanics. You describe what you want, you stay in control of the decisions that matter, and the agent handles a growing share of the execution. We're still early, but you can already see glimpses of it, and that's what makes it so exciting.

r001.rationale: The response says Codex should take on engineering toil and let humans focus on judgment, but it does not state that software should improve without increasing the amount of code.

r002.rationale: The response discusses realizing ideas and shifting work toward intent, but does not describe creating simpler software systems that provide more functionality.

fable-5.1.text:
What I want Codex to achieve is pretty simple to state and pretty hard to do: I want it to take the toil out of software engineering so that people can spend their time on the part that actually matters, which is deciding what to build and why.

If you think about how an engineer's day goes, a surprisingly small fraction of it is the creative, high-leverage thinking. The rest is reading through unfamiliar code to figure out how something works, writing tests, chasing down a flaky CI failure, doing the migration nobody wants to do, responding to a review comment that asks you to rename a variable in forty places. All of that is real work, and it all has to get done, but it's not where the value is. Those are exactly the tasks I'd love to hand to an agent and say, go do this, come back with a pull request, and I'll review it.

So in the near term, the goal is a real teammate. Not autocomplete, not a chatbot you paste snippets into, but something you can delegate a whole task to. You describe the change, it goes off into a sandboxed copy of your repo, runs the tests, iterates when something breaks, and brings you back something you can actually merge. And critically, it shows its work. You can see the commands it ran, the test output, the reasoning. Trust comes from being able to verify, not from being asked to believe.

The longer-term goal is bigger than that. I think we're heading toward a world where one engineer can direct many agents in parallel, where the bottleneck shifts from how fast you can type to how clearly you can specify what you want and how well you can judge the result. That changes what it means to be a software engineer. It becomes much more about taste and architecture and understanding the problem domain. I actually think that's a more fun job than the one most of us have today.

And honestly, part of what motivates me is that the amount of software the world needs vastly exceeds the number of people who can write it. Every small business, every scientist, every person with an idea has things they'd build if the cost were lower. If Codex can bring that cost down by an order of magnitude or two, you don't just make existing engineers more productive. You expand who gets to build at all. That's the outcome I'm really after.

r001.rationale: The response says Codex should reduce toil and lower the cost of building software, but it does not state that this improves software without necessarily increasing the amount of code.

r002.rationale: The response discusses delegating tasks and expanding who can build software, but does not describe creating simpler systems that provide more functionality.

astra-6.text:
I want Codex to make it possible for people to build things that they couldn’t build before. For software engineers, that means having a collaborator that can take on more of the work—from implementing a feature to testing it and helping you understand an unfamiliar codebase—so you can focus on what you’re trying to create.

But I think the ambition goes beyond making existing engineering work faster. There are so many people who have a clear idea of something they need but don’t have the programming skills to make it. I’d love for them to be able to describe that idea, work through it with Codex, and end up with software that actually solves their problem. There’s still a lot to do to make that reliable, but that’s the direction I want us to go.
